cites.sentence: Standard theory predicts supply contraction under binding rent ceilings, but the relevant question is empirical, and the evidence is specific: the long-run elasticity of marginal SDU-type supply to controlled rents is estimated at 0.31 to 0.48, meaning a 10 percent cap-induced reduction removes roughly 3 to 5 percent of stock over five years [D6p1].

Critically, the literature distinguishes first-generation controls (hard caps on levels) from second-generation controls (caps on increases within tenancies): the former show consistent contraction, the latter small or null effects [D6p2].

Hong Kong's 2021 ordinance is second-generation, and the stock grew from 100,800 units in 2019 to 111,200 in 2025 through the ordinance period [D2p1]—stability that the working paper explains precisely by the instrument's non-binding character [D6p2].

Hong Kong's 2021 ordinance is second-generation, and the stock grew from 100,800 units in 2019 to 111,200 in 2025 through the ordinance period [D2p1]—stability that the working paper explains precisely by the instrument's non-binding character [D6p2].

In the modelled tightened-cap scenario, a 15 percent cut in initial rents yields a net transfer of about 900 dollars per month to incumbents—but leaves 3,000 to 4,000 households per year unable to enter the segment, mostly new arrivals and newly formed households [D6p4].
Those excluded are the same population the cap intends to protect [D6p3].

Berlin illustrates the mechanism: initial-offer rents fell sharply, but listing supply contracted within a year as owners withheld or rerouted flats, and when the law was struck down the suppressed increases released above the pre-cap trend line [D7p1][D7p2].

Berlin illustrates the mechanism: initial-offer rents fell sharply, but listing supply contracted within a year as owners withheld or rerouted flats, and when the law was struck down the suppressed increases released above the pre-cap trend line [D7p1][D7p2].
The Berlin lesson is explicit—the cap protects those already inside and hands the bill to those still outside [D7p3].

Mr Chan, a delivery driver paying 5,800 dollars for a 120 sq ft cubicle, is split on a hard cap: it would free maybe 800 dollars a month, but he fears landlords would rather convert units back to storage, and he has already seen two units on his floor emptied and locked for a year [D3p1][D3p2].

Mr Chan, a delivery driver paying 5,800 dollars for a 120 sq ft cubicle, is split on a hard cap: it would free maybe 800 dollars a month, but he fears landlords would rather convert units back to storage, and he has already seen two units on his floor emptied and locked for a year [D3p1][D3p2].
Asked what would help most, he does not name rent—he names the waiting list, saying he would accept any rent if the queue were three years instead of five and a half [D3p3].
The NGO survey of 440 households confirms this at scale: 61 percent would trade a nominal rent increase for three-year security of tenure, and 74 percent for a faster public-housing offer [D11p1].
She has lived in an SDU for nine years, has never received a written tenancy agreement, and says the ordinance changed nothing she can see [D4p1].
She supports a hard cap, arguing her building's four SDU landlords would not exit because "where else would the money come from?" [D4p2].

But the interviewer notes a contradiction she does not see: two flats in her stairwell were converted to non-residential storage after the ordinance, even as she believes landlords cannot exit [D4p3].
Current inspection capacity covers under 6 percent of stock per year, and a band-based initial-rent cap requires a certifiable tenancy register estimated at 40 to 60 staff-years to stand up [D10p1].

Worse, if landlords reprice above-band rents, the first instrument tenants hold is complaint—but the tenants least able to complain are those with no written agreement, like Mrs Wong, or the newest arrivals [D10p2].
The subcommittee could not identify any enforcement design under which the newest-arrival tail is protected first rather than last [D10p3].

A hard cap framed as deprivation of income stream would almost certainly attract compensation claims under the Basic Law, while contractual-term regulation sits on firmer ground but leaves initial rent—the actual pain point—unregulated [D9p1].

Counsel's middle instrument, a published per-square-foot band that regulators can defend as rate-capping rather than confiscation, is both legally safer and consistent with the NGO's preferred narrow tightening [D9p2][D11p3].

The counter-argument—that the stable stock under the 2021 ordinance shows capacity for more control [D12p2]—is answered by the elasticity literature itself: that stability is an artifact of a non-binding instrument, and a binding one behaves differently [D6p2].
